name: Oromo
variety: Western and central (Mecha-Tulama) Oromo as written in the Qubee orthography; the tone description follows Harar Oromo (Owens 1985), the best described variety
sources: Owens, Jonathan (1985). A Grammar of Harar Oromo (Northeastern Ethiopia). Hamburg: Buske.
Lloret, Maria-Rosa (1997). Oromo phonology. In Alan S. Kaye (ed.), Phonologies of Asia and Africa. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.
Banti, Giorgio (1988). Two Cushitic systems: Somali and Oromo nouns. In Harry van der Hulst & Norval Smith (eds.), Autosegmental Studies on Pitch Accent. Dordrecht: Foris.
Stroomer, Harry (1995). A Grammar of Boraana Oromo (Kenya). Köln: Rüdiger Köppe.
Gragg, Gene B. (1976). Oromo of Wellegga. In M. Lionel Bender (ed.), The Non-Semitic Languages of Ethiopia. East Lansing: Michigan State University.
Mous, Maarten (2022). The grammatical primacy of tone in Cushitic. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 62.
Al Solami, Majed (2021). The prosody of Harar Oromo nouns. Jurnal Arbitrer 8(2): 107-130.
contrasts: vowel length in all five qualities: hara 'lake' against haaraa 'new'
plain voiceless, voiced and ejective stops and affricates: t d tʼ, k ɡ kʼ, tʃ dʒ tʃʼ
implosive /ɗ/ (written dh) against /d/ and ejective /tʼ/ (written x)
glottal stop (written with an apostrophe, hudhaa) as a full consonant
/p v z/ occur in loanwords only; the labial ejective /pʼ/ (written ph) is infrequent
allophony: /ɗ/ is a voiced retroflex stop, for many speakers with implosive (ingressive glottalic) release [ᶑ]; between vowels it may be a retroflex flap
short vowels are more centralised than the long ones
word-final short vowels are devoiced or whispered before pause in some varieties (reported for Boraana and Harar)
single /r/ is a tap, geminate /rr/ a trill
/n/ takes the place of a following stop; /ln/ becomes [ll]
the stops /t d/ are dental or alveolar; /ɗ/ is further back
the ejectives /tʼ kʼ tʃʼ/ are written x, q, c
phonotactics: no clusters at the beginning or end of a word; at most two consonants meet word-medially
an epenthetic /i/ breaks up three consonants that meet in suffixation
most nouns and adjectives end in a vowel
most consonants may be geminate, word-medially only
vowel length is contrastive in all positions, including the end of the word

stress.type: pitch accent; stress follows the high tone
stress.rule: The first syllable of the word with high pitch is heard as stressed; the high pitch is limited to the last two syllables of the root.
stress.cues: pitch; vowel and consonant length are independent of it

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none; short vowels are slightly centralised and final short vowels are whispered before pause in some varieties
rhythm.notes: No rhythm-metric classification is cited and the final lengthening value is provisional. Quantity is contrastive for vowels and consonants, so durations must be kept apart.

length.notes: Long vowels are written double and geminates with double consonant letters; the digraphs ch, dh, ny, ph, sh are normally not doubled, so their length is not shown in writing. No duration measurements are cited here.

intonation.declarative: the high tones of the words are realised on a declining baseline, with low pitch at the end of the sentence; the verb is final
intonation.yes_no_question: word order of a statement; high or rising pitch on the final syllable
intonation.wh_question: prominence on the question word, falling end
intonation.continuation: non-final clauses end on sustained or rising pitch
intonation.accent_shape: high level on the accented syllable, low before it
intonation.notes: Oromo sentence intonation is little studied; these settings are provisional. Focus and case marking interact with the tone pattern of the word.

tone.tone_bearing_unit: syllable (Banti 1988; the mora in other analyses)

inventory.name: final high
inventory.description: all syllables low except the last, which is high; the digits are schematic (low 2, high 4) and cover the last two syllables

inventory.name: penultimate and final high
inventory.description: the last two syllables high, earlier syllables low; a high penult is never followed by a low final; the digits are schematic

inventory.name: all low
inventory.description: no high tone, for example on a head noun that is followed by a modifier; the digits are schematic

sandhi: a head noun is low throughout when a modifier follows it
the first syllable of certain words takes the opposite tone of the last syllable of the preceding word (alternating tone rule, Owens 1985)
most suffixes that end in a long vowel put a high tone on the preceding syllable
tone.neutral_tone: syllables before the last two of the root are low
tone.notes: Only the last two syllables of a root can carry high tone, so the lexical pattern is an accent rather than a full tone system, but the surface patterns are complex because each morpheme adds its own tones. Tone mainly marks grammar (case, verb forms, focus) and is not written. Descriptions differ between dialects and between syllable-based and mora-based analyses.

phonation: whispered final short vowels before pause in some varieties

problems: dh, the implosive /ɗ/, is the dental fricative [ð]: the phoneme D calls the base phoneme D (English th in this). dhugaa gives [ðuɡaː], haadha gives [haːða].
y, the glide /j/, is sent to a vowel phoneme named y, which the table defines twice (as a front rounded vowel and as a central vowel with the IPA name ?). yaada begins with a vowel instead of [j].
The glottal stop written with an apostrophe is dropped: har'a gives [hara], re'ee gives [reeː].
ph, the ejective /pʼ/, is an unaspirated [p] whose IPA name is Φ; of the ejectives only q uses an ejective recording (ustop/k_ejc), x and c use unaspirated plosive samples after a pause.
No pitch accent. Stress is penultimate, or final when the final vowel is long and the penult short, and it is realised with the default stress contour.
Unstressed short i is changed to a lax [ɪ]; the vowel table contains unused vowels copied from other languages.
good: long vowels and geminates follow the doubled letters, so the quantity contrasts are audible
the ejectives q, x and c are separate phonemes from k, t and ch
ny, ch and sh map to ɲ, tʃ and ʃ

notes: No formant or voice onset time figures are given because none could be checked. The Chao digits in the tone inventory are schematic renderings of low and high, not measured values.
